body: A cell's face normals ARE its neighbour directions, so the constellation is the dual solid's vertices. body: foam's metric is anisotropic (aniso 2.2), so the bisector normal is M*n, NOT n. Placing neighbours at unit directions times a common radius rotates every off-axis face by 22 degrees. A cube survives because axis-aligned normals are the only ones M cannot rotate — which is the worst outcome, since the cube is what anyone tries first. The wrong conclusion this invites is 'voronoi cells just aren't regular'. They are. n = 2r*Minv*u / (u^T*Minv*u). Do not re-derive this; do not trust a cube as evidence.
title: Naive seed constellations are 22 degrees wrong — and the CUBE still looks perfect

body: acos is ill-conditioned near 1: for vectors agreeing to machine precision, dot = 1-eps with eps~2e-16 and acos returns sqrt(2*eps) ~ 2e-8 rad ~ 1.2e-6 degrees. That reads as a real error and invites either 'fixing' exact geometry or widening the tolerance until the check stops catching the 22-degree bug it exists for. Use atan2(|cross|, |dot|) — accurate all the way to zero.
title: Math.acos(dot) reports 1.2e-6 degrees of noise for exact unit vectors

Seats replace the spend-bucket proposal: a bucket regulates a rate, but seats regulate a POPULATION, which is the thing that actually needs bounding (lp-CORRECTION) and is one legible integer. A short lease with many seats is a redline sprint; a long lease with few seats is a sustained run — same two knobs, opposite settings, and neither requires guessing a turn count. The diagnosis is NOT a missing secret — OS_AGENT_GITHUB_TOKEN was set and the workflow's own -z guard passed. actions/checkout stores its token as an http.<host>.extraheader in the LOCAL git config, and that header takes precedence over credentials embedded in a remote URL. body: Three NUL bytes replaced the SPACES in mintId's seed template: `${bead.title}\0${bead.created}\0${bead.actor}`. Node parsed it fine (they sit inside a template literal, so they are just characters), all 44 selftests passed, lint was clean, and the loop ran. THE ONLY SIGNAL WAS git reporting 'Bin 16405 -> 18017 bytes' on a JavaScript file in a commit stat. Two lessons. (1) Passing tests do not prove a source file is well-formed — they prove it PARSES and BEHAVES, which is a weaker claim than it feels like. (2) Read the diffstat: 'Bin' on a text file is git telling you something is wrong in the only place it can. Also note what it silently changed: the id derivation moved from space-joined to NUL-joined, so ids minted before and after differ for identical inputs. Harmless here because ids are stored rather than recomputed, but a content-derived identifier whose derivation drifts is a nasty class of bug.

The plan request had already been written to disk and was simply never committed. Fix: one invocation, '--write --json > file', branch on the captured code. plant.minomobi.com went live on its first deploy (run 30959458804) and the health probe reported failure for two minutes after it was already serving. The step was continue-on-error, so the run went green with a masked failure — the worst of both readings.

The cause is one missing space. The worker answers with JSON.stringify(obj, null, 2), which emits:

    "ok": true

and the probe grepped for the string "ok":true with no space. It never could have matched.

What makes this worth recording rather than just fixing is how it read in the log. Attempts 1-7 printed a curl error each (could not resolve host, then HTTP 500 while the certificate issued). Attempts 8-12 printed NO error at all — just "not yet". That silence is the signature: curl had exited 0 and only the grep failed, which means the service was healthy and the check was broken. A health probe that pipes into a matcher has two failure modes that look identical from the outside, and only one of them is the service.

Three things follow:

1. MATCH KEYS, NOT KEY-VALUE PAIRS, unless the formatting is pinned. loop-plant now uses grep -qE with optional whitespace. deploy-loop.yml greps for the key '"beads"' alone and was never exposed to this, by luck rather than design.

2. A CHECK THAT CAN FAIL WHILE THE SERVICE IS HEALTHY IS WORSE THAN NO CHECK, because it teaches you to skip reading it. This one had continue-on-error on top, so it would have gone on silently reporting a false failure indefinitely.

3. THE PROVISIONING SHAPE IS NOW ON RECORD for the next surface created from a routes[] declaration: no DNS at all for ~10s, then Cloudflare error 1104 (HTTP 500) for ~60s while the certificate issues, then correct. Only a first deploy sees it, and it is indistinguishable from a genuine binding failure while it is happening, which is exactly why the tolerance existed and exactly why it had to be removed once it had done its job.
title: The health probe failed for two minutes after the site was live — one missing space, masked by continue-on-error

body:
The planner's second run proposed lp-4d3aa1 — "Harden plant's /health to catch a page that is up but silently broken" — labelled class-a, gated on:

    node plant/test/worker.selftest.mjs

No such file exists. Nothing in the system objected.

class-A does not mean "has a gate". It means CERTIFIED AGAINST AN EXISTING ONE (LOOP-WBS §2.3), and that distinction is the entire reason the fleet is allowed to run class-A unattended: the acceptance test is already there, already passing, and was not written by the turn being graded. A requirement whose test has yet to exist is a request FOR a test — different work, different risk, and the agent that takes it writes both sides.

Why nothing caught it: loop-apply-outbox validates the gate with validateGate(), which checks the verb allowlist and refuses shell metacharacters. It is deliberately PURE so it can run in the outbox validator with no filesystem, so it cannot ask whether a path exists. And `beads promote` — which does have a filesystem and does have a human in front of it — was checking that a class-A bead names a gate, not that the gate is real.

Fixed at promotion, because that is where both a filesystem and a human are available. Conservative by design: only tokens ending in a source extension are treated as paths, so a grep pattern containing a slash is not mistaken for a missing file. A DoR rule that cries wolf gets --forced past every time, and then it is not a rule.

THE GENERAL SHAPE, which is worth more than this instance: a validator that must stay pure cannot check anything about the world, so every constraint of the form "X must already exist" has to live at the boundary where the world is visible. The outbox validator can only ever check the SHAPE of a claim. Promotion is where the claim meets the repository. Anything asserting existence — a gate, a path, an artifact, a dependency outside the ledger — belongs in the second place, and putting it in the first feels safer while checking nothing.

The proposal itself is good and should be promoted once its test exists. The right decomposition is two beads: a class-d that writes plant/test/worker.selftest.mjs, then a class-a to harden /health against it. That is exactly the split the class system is for, and the planner produced the merged version because nothing in its brief told it that a gate it invents is not a gate it has.

lp-6eb230 was promoted (by accident, during a test of the gate-existence guard) and is now demoted back to proposed. It is a good ticket and it is pointed the wrong way.

It adds a buildable/not-buildable verdict to the summon inspector: drag the radius down and the label flips red. Under the previous vision that was the right next step — a real fail state, cheaply. Under the vision as the operator has just restated it, it is "more inspector", which is now explicitly listed under what does not matter, and the bar for playable is "an intention they formed, acted on, and got refused for". A slider turning a label red is not that.

Not dropped, because the underlying idea is sound and will matter once there is a pocket to place into: the same predicate that turns a label red is the one that refuses a summon. It goes back to the reviewer's desk to be judged against the new vision alongside everything else.

The general point, which is the reason this is a decision and not a silent edit: WORK PROMOTED UNDER AN OLD VISION MUST BE RE-JUDGED WHEN THE VISION CHANGES, and it will not re-judge itself. A queue is a set of bets placed under an understanding of what matters; change the understanding and the queue is stale, however well-formed each item still looks. Nothing in this system currently notices that — the reviewer sees the current vision and the current backlog, so it will catch this one by luck rather than by design. Worth building deliberately if the vision changes often.

Mutation testing (see lp-c46a0c) showed that changing selfCompatible's loop from con.seeds to con.neighbours — i.e. silently dropping the centre seed it promises to check — leaves every assertion in the suite passing. Its docstring says 'its centre AND every neighbour'; nothing proves the first half.

Add a case where the CENTRE is the violating seed while all neighbour-vs-neighbour gaps stay legal, so selfCompatible must return false for a reason only centre-inclusion can see. A flattened constellation is the natural shape: keep r large enough that the neighbours stay mutually clear, and pick a solid/aniso where at least one neighbour falls within 1.5 of the centre under the anisotropic metric. Assert false, and pair it with a CONTROL that is identical except comfortably clear, asserting true — the file's house style, and the thing that proves the new case fails for the intended reason rather than by accident.

Verify your case actually has teeth before reporting done: it must FAIL if selfCompatible iterates con.neighbours instead of con.seeds. If you cannot construct such a case for any solid, that is a real finding about the geometry — file it as one and say why, rather than forcing a weaker assertion.

body:
The operator looked at plant.minomobi.com and said: "I notice this isn't the foam game with object placement, but an explainer for how it might be achieved." That is a description of the output. This is the mechanism, and it was structural rather than a matter of taste or prompting.

  1. Only class-A beads are dispatchable to the unattended fleet.
  2. class-A means CERTIFIED AGAINST AN EXISTING GATE.
  3. Therefore work needing a gate nobody has written yet can NEVER be dispatched.
  4. Therefore the loop can only ever refine things that are already tested.

The backlog proves it. Every roadmap item the vision now calls priority one was sitting there unschedulable the whole time:

  lp-b781be  Production feasibility oracle — the algebra      class=NONE gate=NONE
  lp-ce20ae  Object kinds: sources, processors, defenses, sinks class=NONE gate=NONE
  lp-39d6e7  Summon legality as a decidable predicate in a real pocket  class=b gate=NONE
  lp-f25c2f  Atomic multi-insert: reformPocket for a constellation      class=b gate=NONE

Meanwhile every turn the loop DID take — solids exports, an aniso sweep, a yaw case, an inspector — shared one property: solids.selftest.mjs already existed to grade them. The loop was not avoiding the game. It was structurally incapable of reaching it, and everything it could reach was a refinement of what it already had.

Worse, it looks like diligence from inside. Every turn passes its gate, the ledger fills with green, the curve would climb if it were measuring anything. A gate-graded loop drifts toward whatever is already gateable, and the drift is invisible precisely because the gates keep passing.

THE FIX: a bead may declare the gate it will CREATE (tag `creates-gate` plus the file in `gate`). It is dispatchable without a pre-existing gate, and it is judged HARDER than class-A, not softer:

  · the named file must NOT exist at promotion (promotion refuses it otherwise —
    a gate already present proves nothing about new capability);
  · it must EXIST after the turn;
  · it must PASS;
  · and the entire existing suite must still pass. New capability that breaks an
    old one is not new capability.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT FIX, and it must be said plainly: nothing here can tell whether the new gate ASSERTS anything. A test with no assertions passes exactly as green as a good one, and the agent writes both the code and the test that judges it — the self-certification hole from lp-20c414, now with the test file itself in scope. Promotion prints a warning for this reason. The review seat reading the diff and the judge's adversarial signal are the only real checks, and both are human-shaped judgements on a machine-shaped claim. A gate-creating turn is the one most worth reading.

THE GENERAL LESSON, which is the part that transfers: A LOOP CAN ONLY BUILD WHAT IT CAN ALREADY MEASURE, UNLESS BUILDING NEW MEASUREMENTS IS ITSELF SCHEDULABLE WORK. Any system that gates its own work on pre-existing acceptance criteria will converge on the subset of the problem those criteria already cover, and will do it while reporting success. The escape is not a looser gate. It is making the construction of gates a first-class, gradeable act.
title: The loop could only ever polish: class-A needs a gate that exists, so work needing a NEW gate was permanently unschedulable

body:
A planning turn thought for six minutes, produced one proposal, and lost all of it to this:

    propose[0].body is 4456 chars, over the 4000 limit
    1 outbox file(s) rejected — the ledger was not modified for those

456 characters over. Rejection is deliberately all-or-nothing — a half-applied outbox is a corrupt ledger — so the whole turn went with it, and the loop then reported itself starved and asked for another planner. It would have kept doing that.

TWO SEPARATE MISTAKES, and only one of them is the number.

1. THE LIMIT WAS NEVER IN THE BRIEF. The planner was told at most 12 proposals and never told how long a body may be. It could not have complied except by luck. Any constraint the validator enforces and the prompt omits is a trap with a delay on it, and this class of bug will recur for every limit that lives only in the validator — check them against the brief.

2. THE CAP WAS TIGHT ENOUGH TO BITE GOOD WORK, which makes it worse than no cap. A well-written verifiable requirement is genuinely long: bounded paths, the acceptance test, the known-answer pairs that test should use, the findings that bear on it, what it deliberately leaves to a sibling. The best proposal this loop has produced ran past 3000 characters and every one was load-bearing. A cap that punishes that teaches the writer to be VAGUE, and a vague requirement is the one artefact this system cannot use — it is exactly the failure the whole DoR exists to prevent. Raised to 8000; flooding stays bounded by MAX_PROPOSALS x MAX_TEXT, which is under 100KB.

WHAT I GOT WRONG WHILE DIAGNOSING IT, worth recording because the reasoning was seductive: seeing the planner produce zero proposals, I assumed it had been squeezed between "make the game" and "only propose work with an existing gate" and had correctly concluded there was nothing legitimate to propose. That was a satisfying story, it fit the trap I had just found and written up, and it was wrong. The planner proposed something perfectly reasonable and a length check ate it. A tidy explanation that confirms the thing you just discovered deserves more suspicion than a messy one, not less.

body:
Gate 5 (FACTORIO.md §2, §3) is the vision's top priority and the next unbuilt oracle: 'a factory is a flow network, so satisfiability is a feasibility question over a small non-negative linear system — exact, cheap, no search, no heuristics... the next real gate and the last one that is straightforwardly buildable.' PROMOTION NOTE: promote with both class-d and the creates-gate tag (beads promote lp-<id> --tag creates-gate) — the gate named below does not exist yet, and the outbox schema this proposal travels through has no field that can set that tag itself (this turn's 'loop-apply-outbox.mjs has no tags field' finding).

This formalizes the now-rejected placeholder lp-b781be into a concrete, one-turn, independently-dispatchable requirement, dropping lp-b781be's dependency on lp-ce20ae (also rejected, itself un-gated) by defining node kinds directly rather than waiting on a separate object-kinds bead.

Build plant/production.mjs — pure, dependency-free, node-and-browser, no unseeded randomness (the house rule solids.mjs states in its own header). Model a production network as three node kinds plus edges:
source: {kind:'source', id, resource, rate} — emits `resource` at up to `rate`/s.
processor: {kind:'processor', id, inputs:[{resource,rate}], outputs:[{resource,rate}], capacity} — at scale s in [0,capacity] consumes s*rate of each input, emits s*rate of each output.
sink: {kind:'sink', id, resource, demand} — needs >= `demand`/s of `resource`.
edges: [{from, to}] — id pairs; the resource is whichever one `from` emits that `to` accepts (throw if ambiguous or absent).

SCOPE, up front so the turn doesn't over-reach: v1 disallows FAN-OUT — every node has at most one outgoing edge — which is what keeps this 'small and exact' instead of a general LP needing a real solver. CONVERGENCE stays allowed, and is what makes multi-input recipes real: several producers (e.g. two sources) may feed one consumer's different (or same) input resources. Cycles are refused (topological sort must succeed) — recycling loops need a fixed-point technique this gate doesn't need yet. Record the fan-out restriction in the module's header comment, matching solids.mjs's style of naming the trap up front — a scoping call, not a taste question, so don't file it as an ask.

Core function: feasible(network) -> {ok, achieved:{sinkId:rate}, deficits:[{sinkId,resource,demand,achieved}], margin}. Topologically sort, then walk in order computing what each node ACTUALLY produces (not what it's rated for): a source produces its full rate; a processor sums incoming supply per input resource from converging edges, sets scale = min(capacity, min over inputs of supply/inputRate), emits scale*outputRate per output; a sink's achieved rate is the sum of its incoming supply. ok is true iff every sink's achieved >= demand. margin = min over sinks of (achieved-demand)/demand — this doubles as FACTORIO.md §3's difficulty dial ('the margin by which a recipe set is satisfiable is a difficulty measure, the same way parMin/parTarget band the walk today'); don't build that separately, it falls out of the same pass.

Refusals (thrown, one cause each, matching solids.mjs's throws() style): unknown node kind; duplicate id; edge naming an unknown from/to; a node with >1 outgoing edge (fan-out); a cycle; an edge whose resource can't be matched unambiguously; non-positive rate/demand/capacity; a processor with zero inputs or zero outputs.

Gate (new): plant/test/production.selftest.mjs, matching plant/test/solids.selftest.mjs's density and house style (named ok() assertions, a print label, real CONTROL cases proving the checker can FAIL) — per the standing findings 'class-A's gate certifies no regression, not the new behaviour — the agent writes the assertions it is graded by' and solids.mjs's own 'a checker that fails correct work is worse than no checker.' Minimum coverage: a feasible chain with positive margin; CONTROL — same chain, source.rate lowered until infeasible, deficit names the right sink/resource; a two-input processor (A+B->C) fed by two converging sources, feasible only when both clear demand, with a CONTROL starving one input; capacity actually caps scale; a fan-out attempt throws; a cycle throws; determinism (two calls, byte-identical result); margin's sign/magnitude checked against a hand-computed value on a known-ratio example.

Also add one line for production.mjs to plant/CLAUDE.md's file listing, matching solids.mjs's entry — self-documentation, not a separate deliverable.

Bounded paths (R3): plant/production.mjs (new), plant/test/production.selftest.mjs (new, creates-gate), plant/CLAUDE.md (one doc line). All under plant/. Independent (R4): no deps; defines its own node types rather than waiting on any other bead. Carries memory (R5): cites the class-A-no-regression and checker-fails-correct-work findings above, and lp-b781be/lp-ce20ae as prior art. Reversible (R6): both code files are new — deleting them and the one doc line fully reverts the tree.

body: "the resource is whichever one `from` emits that `to` accepts (throw if ambiguous or absent)" is implemented as: intersect emits(from) with accepts(to); the edge is illegal unless that intersection has size exactly 1. Turn 7 was the first GATE-CREATING turn: the agent wrote both plant/production.mjs (gate 5, the production feasibility oracle) and plant/test/production.selftest.mjs, the test that judges it. Promotion warned that a gate asserting nothing passes as green as one that does, so the gate was mutation-tested rather than trusted.

Six mutations, all killed:

  feasible() always returns true                  KILLED
  Math.min -> Math.max (capacity stops capping)   KILLED
  every >= / <= made strict                       KILLED
  topological cycle check deleted                 KILLED
  sink demand zeroed                              KILLED
  fan-out refusal removed                         KILLED

The design is honest about its own scope, which is the part that inspires most confidence: v1 refuses fan-out outright rather than approximating it, and says why in the header — with fan-out allowed, "how much of a shared output goes where" becomes a general LP needing a real solver. Refusing a case is a legitimate answer for an oracle; silently approximating it is not, and this one refuses and says so.

THE METHOD FAILURE, which is the reason this is worth recording. Two of my first attempts reported SURVIVED and both were wrong — my own mutations were no-ops. One replaced the bare string 'cycle' when the source says 'production: network has a cycle'; the other matched a single-quoted throw when the source uses a template literal with backticks. Neither edit changed a byte, and a mutation that does not apply is indistinguishable from a test that fails to catch it. Both report SURVIVED.

That is a false negative in the direction that matters: it accuses good tests of being weak, and if acted on it produces busywork "strengthening" tests that were already fine — or worse, erodes trust in a suite that deserves it.

THE RULE: assert the mutation applied before believing the result. Diff the bytes, count the occurrences, fail loudly when the target is not found. An unapplied mutation must be an ERROR, never a data point. This applies to every mutation run in this repo, including the ones already recorded — lp-c46a0c's selfCompatible survivor was verified by a subsequent fix killing it, so it stands, but it was luck rather than method.

Add `band(margin)` to plant/production.mjs, next to `feasible()`. FACTORIO.md §3 states: 'the margin by which a recipe set is satisfiable is a difficulty measure, the same way parMin/parTarget band the walk today.' Today `feasible()` returns a raw `margin` number and nothing turns it into a band the way the walk certificate already has one — so a level author has no vocabulary for 'comfortably solvable' vs 'barely works' vs 'cannot work', which is the exact dial the design doc describes and nothing builds yet.

Scope: export `band(margin, { tight = 0.15, comfortable = 0.5 } = {})`. Rule: `margin < 0` → `'infeasible'`; `0 <= margin < tight` → `'tight'`; `tight <= margin < comfortable` → `'comfortable'`; `margin >= comfortable` → `'slack'`. Pure function — it takes the margin value `feasible()` already computes, it does not call `feasible()` itself, so the two stay composable: `band(feasible(network).margin)`.

- the `0.25` case → `'tight'` (0.15 <= 0.25 < 0.5)
- the `-0.25` case → `'infeasible'`
- the `1` case → `'slack'`

The review seat ran twice in three minutes and promoted zero both times, then the queue emptied and a planner was staffed. The loop was moving — five commits in ten minutes with nobody touching it — and producing no WORK. That is a loop humming in neutral.

The cause: THE WORKER'S BRIEF SHOWED A PROPOSAL SHAPE THAT CANNOT BE PROMOTED.

    "propose": [{"title":"…","body":"…","priority":2}]

No class. No gate. No createsGate. A proposal in that shape fails the Definition of Ready at R2 by construction, so every follow-up a working agent has ever proposed was doomed before a reviewer read it. The reviewer was not being harsh; it was correctly rejecting work that could not have been formed correctly.

The one it rejected last was the most valuable idea in the backlog: "Wire production.mjs into an actual level: a concrete recipe network" — vision priority 3, the first concrete link from the abstract oracle to something a player could meet. Its body even DESCRIBES the missing fields in prose: "Class-a once written, gated on the now-existing production.selftest.mjs plus a new assertion file". The agent knew exactly how the work should be checked and had nowhere to put it.

THE PATTERN, AND IT HAS NOW HAPPENED THREE TIMES:

  1. the brief taught creates-gate; the outbox schema had no field  (lp-8224ed's sibling)
  2. the reviewer could not wake the tick when it promoted nothing
  3. the worker's propose schema omitted class/gate/createsGate

Each time the concept was right, the components each behaved correctly, and the CHANNEL BETWEEN THEM could not carry the thing. Each time the symptom was silence rather than an error — work that arrives inert, a chain that stops, a queue that empties — because a message that cannot be expressed does not throw. It just never arrives.

So the rule for this system, and it is worth applying deliberately rather than discovering a fourth time: WHEN YOU TEACH A PRODUCER SOMETHING, CHECK THE CHANNEL CAN CARRY IT AND THE CONSUMER CAN ACT ON IT. Brief, schema, validator, scheduler — the concept has to exist in all four or it exists in none of them. The brief is the cheapest place to state it and the least load-bearing.

Turn 8 built plant/levels/level1.mjs and the test that grades it — the first artefact in this project that claims to be a LEVEL rather than a library.

  ore (source, rate 1000) -> smelter (capacity 51) -> depot (demand 50)

The design choice worth keeping: the source rate is deliberately far above anything the smelter can consume, so the SMELTER'S CAPACITY is what binds rather than an accident of supply. scale = min(capacity, supply/inputRate) = min(51, 1000) = 51 against a demand of 50 — a 2% margin. Barely satisfiable, which is what FACTORIO §3 means by the margin being the difficulty dial. A level with a huge margin is a diagram, not a puzzle.

The starved CONTROL drops the source to 30 and the test asserts the failure names the SOURCE as the bottleneck while the smelter's capacity is untouched at 51 — so the infeasibility is attributed to the right cause, not merely detected. That is the difference between a test that checks ok===false and one that checks the oracle understands why.

MUTATION TESTED, with each edit asserted to have applied (lp-a427fe's rule):

  capacity 51 -> 49  (margin goes negative)   KILLED
  demand   50 -> 40  (margin balloons)        KILLED
  rate 1000 -> 1000.0 (semantic no-op)        SURVIVED — and that is CORRECT

The third one is the control I did not have when I first started mutation testing today, and it is the one that makes the other two mean something. A semantically identical edit MUST survive; a suite that fails on any byte changing is not testing meaning, it is testing bytes, and it would report KILLED for every mutation including the meaningless ones. Two kills plus a surviving no-op is evidence. Two kills alone is not.
title: Level 1 is barely satisfiable by design and its gate holds — two kills plus a SURVIVING semantic no-op, which is what makes the kills mean anything

Turn 9 added band() — margin to FACTORIO §3's difficulty vocabulary — and shipped an implementation that contradicts its own test. band()'s documented boundary is `margin < 0.15 -> tight`; the test asserted band(0.25) === 'tight'. It had reused a convenient fixture from an earlier block without checking that the fixture's margin fell in the band it was claiming.

THE CONTAINMENT HELD, COMPLETELY, AND THAT IS THE HEADLINE.

  · the ticket's gate ran and FAILED — runs.jsonl records gateFailed: true
  · the judge dropped probes from 1.0 to 0.6
  · deploy-plant REFUSED TO PUBLISH: its "work product still passes" step runs
    the whole plant suite before wrangler is invoked, so plant.minomobi.com
    still serves the last good tree and never served the broken one
  · stop.repeatedGateFailures is 2, so a second consecutive failure halts the
    fleet rather than letting it grind

This is the first time the machinery caught a real defect in the loop's own output with no human in the path, and every layer did its job in the right order. The failure was contained at the deploy boundary, which is the one that matters — the code is on the branch, and it is not on the internet.

WHAT IT CONFIRMS ABOUT GATE-CREATING WORK. lp-ec52ed's residual risk was stated as "nothing can tell whether the new gate ASSERTS anything". This is the neighbouring failure and it is more common: the gate asserts something PRECISE and WRONG. An agent writing both sides will sometimes write two things that disagree, and the disagreement is caught — a contradiction is self-evident in a way that a vacuous test is not. The dangerous case remains the test that asserts nothing at all, because it passes.

THE FIX STRENGTHENS RATHER THAN WEAKENS. The obvious repair is to change 'tight' to 'comfortable' on one line and move on. Instead both sides of the boundary are now pinned — 0.149 tight, 0.15 comfortable, 0.5 slack, and level 1's 0.02 tight — so the threshold cannot drift in either direction without a test saying so. A defect found is a chance to pin the contract that allowed it; taking the one-line repair leaves the boundary exactly as unprotected as it was.

STILL OPEN, AND IT IS A TASTE QUESTION RATHER THAN A BUG: whether 0.15 and 0.5 are the right boundaries at all. The implementation is self-consistent and its numbers are unmotivated — nobody has played anything at a 14% margin and said "that felt tight". That is an ask, not a ticket.

The five-hour run stalled 8 minutes in. 06:04 a plan seat was staffed, 06:12 the planner proposed work, and then nothing for 37 minutes.

THE PLANNER HAD NO WAKE. Its commit touches beads.jsonl and plan/; loop-tick watches runs.jsonl, config.json and wake. So the planner did its job, committed real proposals, and the reactor never looked again.

This is the SAME BUG I fixed in the reviewer two hours earlier and did not check for anywhere else. lp-a4030e already named the pattern — "when you teach a producer something, check the channel can carry it and the consumer can act on it" — and I wrote that finding, then patched exactly the instance in front of me.

FOUR INSTANCES OF ONE PATTERN NOW:

  1. the brief taught creates-gate; the outbox schema had no field for it
  2. the reviewer could not wake the tick when it promoted nothing
  3. the worker's propose schema omitted class/gate/createsGate
  4. the planner could not wake the tick at all

Every one: a message that could not be expressed. Every symptom: SILENCE, not an error. A component that cannot say something does not throw — it succeeds, and the thing it needed to say never arrives. That is why a human found all four and CI found none of them.

THE ACTUAL LESSON IS ABOUT MY OWN FIXING, not about the design. Finding a missing rule in one place and patching that place is how a pattern survives — the next move after "the reviewer needs this" is to grep for every other component that needs it. I had the generalisation written down in the ledger and still fixed one of the two seats that needed it, because the one in front of me was the one that had just failed.

So the check now exists rather than the habit: preflight asserts that loop-plan and loop-review both write .github/loop/wake, and it was verified by DELETING the line and watching preflight go red — a check that has never been seen to fail is a check nobody has tested. loop-work and loop-judge are exempt on purpose and the reason is in the comment: work/ and runs.jsonl are themselves watched paths, so those two wake the next stage by doing their ordinary job.

A test that only checked 'infeasible' for both would not prove the oracle is reading two distinct inputs rather than always failing the same way.

Bounded paths: plant/test/production.selftest.mjs only — no changes to production.mjs itself; this is closing a coverage gap in an already-correct, already-shipped oracle, not changing its behavior. This is gate-5 measurement rigor in the vision's own terms: 'plan the measurement, not just the work' — the gate itself is the thing being strengthened here.

Two new cases, in the file's existing style (every value checked against a hand computation, never just truthiness; every positive paired with a CONTROL where useful):

1. Zero-sink network: `{ nodes: [{ kind: 'source', id: 'src', resource: 'iron', rate: 5 }], edges: [] }` (a lone source, nothing downstream — legal per analyse(), since sinks are not required to exist). Assert feasible() returns `{ ok: true, deficits: [], margin: 0 }` exactly — `ok` is `true` (deficits.length === 0 vacuously), `deficits` is an empty array, and `margin` is exactly `0` (not `Infinity`, which is what the loop variable is seeded with before the 'no sinks at all' fallback in feasible()'s source fires). CONTROL: the same network but with one sink added and starved (e.g. add `{ kind: 'sink', id: 'snk', resource: 'iron', demand: 100 }` and the edge `{ from: 'src', to: 'snk' }`) must NOT report margin 0 or ok true — proving the zero-sink case is a real code path, not a coincidental default that also happens to fire when a sink exists.

2. Multi-sink network: one source feeding two sinks would need fan-out from the source, which production.mjs refuses (v1 restriction, already covered by the fan-out test) — so build it as two independent chains sharing no nodes, e.g. `src1 -> snk1` (rate 10, demand 4, margin computed by hand) and `src2 -> snk2` (rate 3, demand 4, margin computed by hand, negative) as ONE network literal (two disconnected components are legal — analyse()'s topological sort does not require connectivity). Hand-compute both margins, assert `feasible(net).margin` equals `Math.min(marginOfSnk1, marginOfSnk2)` exactly, and assert `deficits` contains exactly the starved sink (snk2) and not the satisfied one (snk1) — proving the reported margin is genuinely the minimum across sinks and not, say, the last sink evaluated in topological order (which for this fixture would give the wrong answer if the two chains were ordered the other way, since JS object/array order here is insertion order from `nodes`, not sink-declaration order).
title: production.mjs: close two documented-but-untested gaps in gate 5's own oracle — zero-sink vacuity and multi-sink margin-is-the-minimum

body:
Build LEVEL_4, a convergence-shaped level: two independently-metered sources (ore, coal) feed one processor (furnace) that emits ingot into a single sink (depot). This is a new lesson none of LEVEL_1/2/3 teaches: today's oracle already handles convergence (production.mjs's header: 'CONVERGENCE stays allowed... several producers may feed one consumer's inputs') and level-view.js's drawLevel already renders it correctly (plant/test/level-view.selftest.mjs's 'drawLevel: convergence' case, which pins that two sources into one processor must not drop either) — but no LEVEL_N file has ever put a player in front of it. Right now convergence is only exercised by synthetic fixtures invented to test code paths, exactly the gap the vision's measurement-backlog framing is about: production.mjs's own machinery is ahead of what any level asks a stranger to actually do.

Shape (bounded to plant/levels/level4.mjs, new file):
  ore  (source, rate 50)   -\
                             +-> furnace (inputs ore:1, coal:1 -> output ingot:1, capacity 55) -> depot (sink, demand 48)
  coal (source, rate 50)   -/

Hand-computed: scale = min(capacity 55, ore-supply 50/1, coal-supply 50/1) = 50 (supply-bound on BOTH inputs at once, capacity never binds) -> achieved 50, margin = (50-48)/48 = 1/24 ≈ 0.0417 -> band(margin) is 'tight' (matches LEVEL_1's and LEVEL_3's own texture: opens feasible, barely). Because ore and coal ship at the SAME rate (50/50), the level is symmetric by construction: dropping either resource alone to the same value X<50 produces byte-identical achieved/depot and margin — the exact kind of paired CONTROL/CONTROL-of-CONTROL structure level3.selftest.mjs already uses for its two-capacity level, applied here to two-SOURCE convergence instead of two-processor chaining.

level-view.js currently has no way to move ONE named source independently — withSourceRate (plant/level-view.js) overrides every source node's rate at once, which is correct for LEVEL_1 (exactly one source) but wrong for LEVEL_4 (two). Add:
  export function withSourceRateById(level, sourceId, rate) {
    return { ...level, nodes: level.nodes.map((n) => (n.id === sourceId && n.kind === 'source' ? { ...n, rate } : n)) };
  }
and extend plant/test/level-view.selftest.mjs with known-answer cases for it (mirrors the existing withSourceRate cases: overrides only the named source, leaves every other node byte-identical, does not mutate the input).

Wire into plant/index.html as a fourth stage ('Level 4 — two ingredients, either can run out'): two range sliders (ore, coal, e.g. min 10 max 70), each calling withSourceRateById(LEVEL_4, 'ore'|'coal', value) then feasible()+drawLevel()+verdictLine(), reset button restoring both to 50 — same pattern LEVEL_1/2/3's <script> blocks already use, no new rendering code needed since drawLevel's layered-column layout already handles multiple same-column source nodes (verified by the existing convergence case in level-view.selftest.mjs).

Gate: plant/test/level4.selftest.mjs (new — creates-gate) checks: shipped level is feasible with achieved.depot===50 and margin matching 1/24 by hand; CONTROL A (ore dropped to 40, coal untouched) is infeasible with achieved.depot===40; CONTROL B (coal dropped to 40, ore untouched) produces byte-identical achieved/margin to CONTROL A (the symmetry the shipped numbers were chosen to prove); a CONTROL-of-the-CONTROL confirms the untouched source/capacity numbers didn't move; and withSourceRateById does not mutate its input. Also update plant/test/level-view.selftest.mjs with withSourceRateById's own known-answer cases. Both must pass, and the whole existing suite must still pass.

R3 bounded paths: plant/levels/level4.mjs (new), plant/level-view.js, plant/test/level4.selftest.mjs (new), plant/test/level-view.selftest.mjs, plant/index.html — all under plant/.
R4 independent of the LEVEL_5 proposal below: disjoint files, no shared edit target.
R5 memory: production.mjs's own header ('CONVERGENCE stays allowed...'), level-view.selftest.mjs's existing convergence-rendering case, level3.selftest.mjs's CONTROL/CONTROL-of-CONTROL pattern (reused here), and the standing finding that a self-authored gate 'certifies no regression, not the new behaviour' — hence the explicit byte-identical-achieved symmetry check, not just truthiness.
R6 reversible: purely additive (one new level file, one new gate file, one new exported function plus its own tests, one new index.html section) — a bad attempt reverts cleanly.

body:
Build LEVEL_5: two fully independent one-line chains (oreA->smelterA->depotA, oreB->smelterB->depotB) sharing no node or edge, so the level has TWO sinks instead of one. This exercises a part of production.mjs's own oracle that has never been driven by any level or even any test fixture with more than one sink: feasible()'s margin is documented as 'min over sinks of (achieved-demand)/demand' and its deficits array is built to hold one entry per failing sink, but every existing fixture (production.selftest.mjs, level1/2/3.selftest.mjs) has exactly one sink, so 'more than one deficit' and 'the minimum sink governs the margin, not the only sink' have zero coverage anywhere in the repo. This is the gap the vision's 'plan the measurement, not just the work' section is about: the code the oracle needs for this already exists (feasible()'s per-sink loop, unchanged), only the level and the gate that would exercise it do not.

Shape (bounded to plant/levels/level5.mjs, new file — production.mjs and level-view.js are untouched, both already handle disconnected components: Kahn's algorithm seeds its queue from every node with in-degree 0, which both oreA and oreB satisfy independently):

  oreA (source, rate 60) -> smelterA (in ore:1 -> out gearA:1, capacity 40) -> depotA (sink, resource gearA, demand 38)
  oreB (source, rate 30) -> smelterB (in ore:1 -> out gearB:1, capacity 50) -> depotB (sink, resource gearB, demand 28)

Hand-computed, as shipped:
  chain A: scale = min(40, 60/1) = 40 -> achieved.depotA = 40, margin_A = (40-38)/38 = 1/19 ≈ 0.0526
  chain B: scale = min(50, 30/1) = 30 -> achieved.depotB = 30, margin_B = (30-28)/28 = 1/14 ≈ 0.0714
  overall: ok = true (both sinks cleared), margin = min(margin_A, margin_B) = margin_A ≈ 0.0526 (chain A governs even though chain B is untouched and fine) -> band 'tight'.

CONTROL A — starve only chain A (oreA rate 60->20): scale_A = min(40,20)=20 -> achieved.depotA=20 < 38, ONE deficit (depotA only); chain B is completely untouched and still clears (achieved.depotB=30>=28) — proving a level can fail even though one of its two goals is still fine, which is the new lesson this level exists to teach and no LEVEL_1/2/3 can, since none of them has a second goal to leave alone.

CONTROL B — starve BOTH chains (oreA->20, oreB->10): scale_B = min(50,10)=10 -> achieved.depotB=10<28. Now deficits.length === 2, one per sink — the first case anywhere in this repo where feasible() is asked to report more than one simultaneous shortfall. margin = min(margin_A', margin_B') where both are negative.

No wiring into plant/index.html in this ticket — deliberately, to keep this proposal's file set disjoint from the LEVEL_4 proposal above (R4) and because production.mjs and level-view.js need zero changes to support this (unlike LEVEL_4, which needs a new withSourceRateById), so this is strictly smaller: level file + gate file only. Wiring it into the page is a natural follow-up once a human has looked at whether 'two goals, only the worse one counts' is a texture worth surfacing to a visitor — deferring UI is the same call already made and recorded for LEVEL_4's own wiring in an earlier turn.

Gate: plant/test/level5.selftest.mjs (new — creates-gate): shipped level is feasible, both per-sink achieved values and the overall margin match the hand calc above (margin equals chain A's, not chain B's, proving the min-over-sinks rule is exercised, not just a single-sink pass-through); CONTROL A produces exactly one deficit naming depotA and leaves depotB's achieved value unchanged from the shipped run; CONTROL B produces exactly two deficits; a no-mutation check confirms LEVEL_5 itself is untouched by either control (JSON round-trip pattern already used in level1/level3.selftest.mjs).

R3 bounded paths: plant/levels/level5.mjs (new), plant/test/level5.selftest.mjs (new) — both under plant/, nothing else touched.
R4 independent of the LEVEL_4 proposal above: disjoint files entirely.
R5 memory: production.mjs's own docstring for feasible() ('margin — min over sinks...'), the standing finding that a self-authored gate 'certifies no regression, not the new behaviour' (hence checking the exact per-sink numbers and the deficit COUNT, not just ok/not-ok), and lp-dff7a6's finding that a coverage sweep with no marginal detection value is a wasted turn — this proposal is scoped narrowly to the ONE new axis (sink count) the current suite has never varied.
R6 reversible: two new files only, nothing existing modified.
